title: Battle at Heaven's Eastern Gate
subtitle: Indra challenges Krishna for the Parijata tree
story:
Krishna came to heaven the way daylight comes to a garden — openly, and before the eyes of everyone.

He had left Dwaraka that morning under the pretext of a hunt, riding out to the Raivataka mountain with Satyaki beside him. There he handed his chariot to his charioteer Daruka, told him to wait and groom the horses, and promised to re-enter the city on that very car by evening. Then, with Satyaki, he mounted the back of Garuda, and his son Pradyumna followed behind in a car swift enough to course over hills. Within the twinkle of an eye the lord of Dwaraka stood in the Nandana forest, the pleasure park of the gods, where hosts of celestial warriors kept watch with their weapons and the finest trees of heaven grew in long, ordered avenues.

He did not linger. Before the guards could gather themselves, Krishna tore the Parijata tree from the earth and set it on Garuda's back. And then a strange thing happened: the tree itself seemed to awaken, to bow before the lord who had taken it, as a living thing might bow in prayer. Krishna spoke to it gently. "Do not fear, O tree." When he was sure it was firmly placed, he circled the stronghold of the gods once, the great tree riding behind him on the king of birds, its branches still heavy with blossoms.

The keepers of the garden did not wait to see more. They ran to Indra with the news, and the sound of their running reached the court of the king of the gods before their words did: the finest tree in heaven was being carried away.

The king of the gods came out mounted on his great elephant Airavata, with his son Jayanta following on a chariot, and found Krishna at the eastern gate of heaven. "O slayer of Madhu," Indra called out, "what is this going on?"

Krishna, seated on Garuda, bowed his head in salute to his elder. "I am only taking away this excellent tree," he said, "for a ceremonious observance for your sister-in-law."

But Indra had given his answer to Narada, and he would not soften it now. "O lotus-eyed one, you should not take away this tree without challenging me to fight. Deal the first blow on me, O mighty-armed Kesava — let your promise be fulfilled by hurling your Kaumodaki mace at me."

So the brothers began. Krishna loosed arrows fierce as thunder at the great elephant; Indra loosed arrows of heavenly make at Garuda and cut off Krishna's shafts as they flew. Krishna, smiling, cut off Indra's in turn, and the two lords of earth and sky stood in the air severing each other's arrows, bowstring answering bowstring. At the twang of the Sharanga and the thunder of Indra's bow together, the inhabitants of heaven themselves swooned away.

While the duel raged, Jayanta slipped toward Garuda and tried to pull the Parijata from the bird's back. "Prevent him," Krishna said to Pradyumna, and instantly his son turned and barred the way. The two young warriors faced each other from their chariots, Jayanta piercing Pradyumna with sharp arrows, Pradyumna answering shaft for shaft, until a fierce combat blazed between the son of Indra and the son of Krishna, as though the quarrel of the fathers had passed whole into the hands of the sons. The gods and the sages, the Siddhas and the Charanas, all looked on, struck with wonder at what they saw.

And then, from the host of heaven, a new champion began to advance — a messenger of the gods named Pravara, of great strength, making straight for the tree on Garuda's back. Krishna marked him and spoke one quiet word to Satyaki. "Even from this place, oppose him." Satyaki, who had never refused his lord, moved to meet the champion of heaven.
reflection: The battle begins with courtesies — Krishna salutes his elder before trading arrows with him — and what follows is a family quarrel fought with divine weapons, watched by all of heaven. The courtesy makes the rupture more striking: neither brother wants to begin the enmity, and neither will step back.
tradition_note: The Vishnu Purana tells this episode differently: there, Krishna disarms the gods with his discus and spares Indra, while the Harivamsha has Indra ride out on Airavata and demand a formal battle. This story follows the Harivamsha.
content_note: An archery battle between Krishna and Indra and their sons; described without gore.
next_story_tease: But the gods had one more champion — a warrior whom no weapon could slay.
hero_scene: At the eastern gate of heaven, Krishna stands on Garuda's back with the uprooted Parijata tree balanced behind him, facing Indra mounted on the great elephant Airavata, while arrows flash between them through the golden light of the celestial city.
